documents.prompt: Graph the SYSTEM $y\ge {{m1}}x{{b1|signed}}$ and $y\le {{m2}}x{{b2|signed}}$. Construct both boundaries and the overlapping solution region.

solutionReview.headline: Graph each boundary with its own style and side, then keep only the region that satisfies both.
reasoning: First inequality $y\ge {{m1}}x{{b1|signed}}$: the boundary passes through $(0,{{b1}})$ and $(1,{{p1}})$. $\ge$ includes equality, so the line is solid; shade above it.
Second inequality $y\le {{m2}}x{{b2|signed}}$: the boundary passes through $(0,{{b2}})$ and $(1,{{p2}})$. $\le$ includes equality, so the line is solid; shade below it.

The solution is the overlap: above the first line AND below the second. The first line rises (slope ${{m1}}$) and the second falls (slope ${{m2}}$), so the overlap is the wedge to the left of where they cross.
Check $(0,{{t}})$: ${{t}}\ge {{b1}}$ and ${{t}}\le {{b2}}$ are both true, so this point is in the overlap.
solutionReview.commonError: Shading everything that satisfies either inequality. The point $(0,{{u}})$ is above the first line, but ${{u}}\le {{b2}}$ is false, so it is not a solution.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Solid $y={{m1}}x{{b1|signed}}$ shaded above, solid $y={{m2}}x{{b2|signed}}$ shaded below; only the overlapping wedge, which contains $(0,{{t}})$, is the solution.

attemptFeedback: Do not stop after one inequality; the final region must satisfy both at once.
supportHints: Build one boundary and shade first, then repeat for the second inequality and keep only the overlap.

variants.prompt: Graph the SYSTEM $y\ge {{lower}}$ and $y\le {{upper}}$. Construct both horizontal solid boundaries and shade only the overlap between them.

solutionReview.headline: Two horizontal inequalities create a horizontal strip between $y={{lower}}$ and $y={{upper}}$.
reasoning: $y\ge {{lower}}$: the boundary is the horizontal line $y={{lower}}$, through $(0,{{lower}})$ and $(1,{{lower}})$. $\ge$ includes equality, so it is solid; shade above it.
$y\le {{upper}}$: the boundary is the horizontal line $y={{upper}}$, through $(0,{{upper}})$ and $(1,{{upper}})$. $\le$ includes equality, so it is solid; shade below it.
Keep only the overlap: the strip ${{lower}}\le y\le {{upper}}$, which is {{gap}} units tall and includes both lines.
Check $(0,{{t}})$: ${{lower}}\le {{t}}\le {{upper}}$ is true, so it is in the strip.
solutionReview.commonError: Keeping the whole region above $y={{lower}}$. The point $(0,{{u}})$ satisfies $y\ge {{lower}}$, but ${{u}}\le {{upper}}$ is false, so it is not a solution.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Solid lines $y={{lower}}$ and $y={{upper}}$, with only the strip ${{lower}}\le y\le {{upper}}$ shaded.

attemptFeedback: Graph each horizontal boundary separately, then keep only the region satisfying both.
supportHints: For y≥constant shade above; for y≤constant shade below.

variants.prompt: Construct the solution graph of $y\ge {{m1}}x{{b1|signed}}$ and $y<{{m2}}x{{b2|signed}}$. Both slopes are fractional. Use exact rise/run, distinguish the solid and dashed boundaries, and shade only the common region.

solutionReview.headline: Build each fractional-slope boundary from its rise and run, give each its own style and side, then keep the overlap.
reasoning: First inequality $y\ge \frac{{{rise1}}}{{{run1}}}x{{b1|signed}}$: from $(0,{{b1}})$, a rise of {{rise1}} over a run of {{run1}} reaches $({{run1}},{{q1}})$. $\ge$ includes equality, so the line is solid; shade above it.

Second inequality $y<\frac{{{rise2}}}{{{run2}}}x{{b2|signed}}$: from $(0,{{b2}})$, a rise of {{rise2}} over a run of {{run2}} reaches $({{run2}},{{q2}})$. $<$ is strict, so the line is dashed; shade below it.
The solution is the overlap: above the first line AND below the second. The first line rises and the second falls, so the overlap is the wedge to the left of where they cross.
Check $(0,{{t}})$: ${{t}}\ge {{b1}}$ and ${{t}}<{{b2}}$ are both true, so this point is in the overlap.
solutionReview.commonError: Shading everything that satisfies either inequality. The point $(0,{{u}})$ is above the first line, but ${{u}}<{{b2}}$ is false, so it is not a solution.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Solid boundary through $(0,{{b1}})$ and $({{run1}},{{q1}})$ shaded above, dashed boundary through $(0,{{b2}})$ and $({{run2}},{{q2}})$ shaded below; only the overlap is the solution.

attemptFeedback: Do not let the fractional slopes distract from the separate boundary-style and shading decisions.
supportHints: Plot each boundary from its y-intercept and exact rise/run before shading.

documents.prompt: A student graphs $y>{{m1}}x{{b1|signed}}$ and $y\le {{m2}}x{{b2|signed}}$ but shades the UNION of the two half-planes. Correct the error by constructing both graphs and showing only the system's overlap.

solutionReview.headline: A system is solved by the intersection of the two half-planes, not their union.
reasoning: First inequality $y>{{m1}}x{{b1|signed}}$: the boundary passes through $(0,{{b1}})$ and $(1,{{p1}})$. $>$ is strict, so the line is dashed; shade above it.
Second inequality $y\le {{m2}}x{{b2|signed}}$: the boundary passes through $(0,{{b2}})$ and $(1,{{p2}})$. $\le$ includes equality, so the line is solid; shade below it.

The student's union also shades points such as $(0,{{u}})$: it is above the first line, but ${{u}}\le {{b2}}$ is false, so it fails the second inequality. A system keeps only points that satisfy both, so erase everything outside the overlap.

The solution is the overlap: above the first line AND below the second. The first line rises (slope ${{m1}}$) and the second falls (slope ${{m2}}$), so the overlap is the wedge to the left of where they cross.
Check $(0,{{t}})$: ${{t}}>{{b1}}$ and ${{t}}\le {{b2}}$ are both true, so this point is in the overlap.
solutionReview.commonError: Shading the union, which also includes points that satisfy only one inequality. Test a point in each shaded piece: it must make both inequalities true.
solutionReview.answerSummary: Dashed $y={{m1}}x{{b1|signed}}$ shaded above, solid $y={{m2}}x{{b2|signed}}$ shaded below; only the overlapping wedge, which contains $(0,{{t}})$, is the solution.
